question.text: A callable bond is most likely to be called by the issuer when:

answer.text: Interest rates rise significantly in the market
Interest rates fall significantly in the market
The company's credit rating is downgraded
The bond is trading at a discount to par

explanation.text: The Logic: The issuer calls the bond when rates for similar bonds fall, because refinancing at a lower cost becomes possible. This creates reinvestment risk for investors, who receive par value and must reinvest at the lower prevailing rates (NISM-Series-X-A, pp.153-155). The Trap: Rising rates would make the existing bond cheaper for the issuer to keep outstanding — there's no incentive to call when refinancing would cost more. Note: A credit downgrade or a discount price does not, by itself, trigger an issuer call; the economic motivation to call is driven by the ability to refinance at lower cost.
